articles.title_zh: Air travel starts to normalize after ground stop caused weekend of unprecedented disruption
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Robert Pattinson named as newest James Bond
Air travel across the United States was largely returning to normal Monday, although some disruption persisted as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule after a rare nationwide ground stop .
The extraordinary shutdown saw thousands of fed up passengers stranded, some sleeping in terminals and missing meetings and family occasions. The fallout from Friday’s stoppage was still being felt, with officials blaming a router issue that derailed air traffic control communications.
But by 9 a.m. ET Monday, about 1,500 flights into and out of the U.S. were delayed and nearly 300 canceled, a dramatic drop from the 10,987 delayed and 2,336 canceled U.S. flights Sunday, according to the aviation data site FlightAware.
American Airlines had the largest number of canceled flights Monday at 157, followed by SkyWest with 38 flights. Dallas-Fort Worth International and Chicago O’Hare International were the origin airports experiencing the highest number of cancellations  Monday, according to data from FlightAware.
However, the outlook for the coming days is set to improve with just 3 U.S. flights due to be canceled Tuesday, as passengers gear up for busy Thanksgiving travel later this month.
“It takes some time for the airlines to rechoreograph all of their crews and aircraft. We’re going to start seeing things get better today, but I think back to normal tomorrow,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday.
The nationwide ground stop lasted several hours Friday and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country.
The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. It was the longest nationwide halt to U.S. air travel since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the United States. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack.
Duffy on Sunday declined to apologize for the ground stop, instead blaming his predecessors and previous presidential administrations that he said did not do enough to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system.
“It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or in decades,” Duffy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “But I can’t apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats because it’s all of them.”
FAA contractor L3Harris had been working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Duffy said Sunday that the replacement triggered problems with another recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other air traffic control centers across the country.
The FAA said it still does not know what ultimately caused the problem that occurred with maintenance work that had been done thousands of times ​before without issue, Duffy added.
Copper-to-fiber optic telecommunications conversions are being completed at FAA facilities around the country at a rapid pace. More than 3,500 communication lines have been replaced out of the 5,170 slated to be switched out by 2028, according to FAA data.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the surge overwhelmed routers at one center and then spread to backup routers at other locations. He said the FAA halted departures to relieve pressure on the system while officials worked to identify the source of the problem.
“I think that was the right call,” Bedford said. “We stand behind that.” Officials are investigating why the router behaved that way.
Friday’s disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a U.S. air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.
President Donald Trump on Sunday called for additional funding from lawmakers, while senior Democrats were skeptical of pleas for more money, pointing to unspent funds. Duffy said that the money unspent last year was earmarked only for certain spending, and did not include funds for new software to manage the airspace.

articles.title_orig: Tributes as wife and daughter of DUP chairman die hours apart
articles.title_zh: Tributes as wife and daughter of DUP chairman die hours apart
articles.content_orig:
Sympathies have been expressed to a senior Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politician following the death of his wife and daughter within hours of each other.
The party said Lord Morrow, who is chairman of the DUP, lost his wife Lady Jennifer Morrow and their daughter Rachel Burrows at the weekend.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that "words cannot adequately express the heartbreak and sorrow felt across our party".
"There are no words that can ease the pain of such an unimaginable loss," he added.
Lord Morrow is a former Stormont minister and a former assembly member for the Fermanagh and South Tyrone constituency.
A funeral notice for his daughter Rachel said she was a married mother of two children. It said she died on Sunday "peacefully surrounded by her loving family".
Robinson added that Lord Morrow's wife and daughter died "within hours of each other" on Sunday.
"On behalf of the Democratic Unionist Party, I extend our deepest sympathy to Maurice, to Rachel's husband John, and to the entire Morrow and Burrows families at this most difficult of times," he said.
"Maurice Morrow has been a rock of strength and support to so many of us through difficult moments in our lives. Now, in his darkest hour, it is our turn to be a rock for him.
"Throughout Jennifer and Rachel's long battles, Maurice has demonstrated extraordinary love and strength."
Speaking at Stormont, Robinson said the last couple of weeks for Lord Morrow would "have been incredibly difficult".
"But to lose your daughter and know how gravely ill your wife is, and to lose your wife some four hours later yesterday, is a deep personal shock and tragedy for him, for his surviving daughter Victoria, for Rachel's husband John and their two children, and for the wider Morrow and Burrows family."
Robinson said that as party chairman for the last 26 years, Lord Morrow has been "steadfast and fundamental to the foundations of the DUP".
"The commitment that runs through us runs through Maurice, and so this time all of us are here as colleagues to pay tribute to Maurice, to offer him comfort and prayers," he added.
Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister also extended his sympathies to Lord Morrow and expressed "sincere Christian condolences".

articles.title_orig: I went to a math class at Caltech. The professor no longer grades homework because everyone's using AI.
articles.title_zh: I went to a math class at Caltech. The professor no longer grades homework because everyone's using AI.
articles.content_orig:
Professor Yi Ni had no laptop or projector. He instead rapidly filled eight blackboards with chalk scrawl during an introductory math class at Caltech on Friday.
Though the instruction was entirely analog, the specter of AI loomed large.
Ni, a professor at Caltech for 17 years, told me that he no longer grades homework on accuracy because students are using AI to complete it. Now, he grades it only on completion.
"There is a problem in the education process," Ni said. "Virtually all the homework in college math, you can use AI."
Chatbots, once derided for their inability to perform such basic tasks as counting the r's in "strawberry," can now do math as well as a graduate student.
And if you're an undergraduate student, that's kind of a big deal. Some, Business Insider has reported, are reconsidering whether to study math at all .
From my perch near the back of the lecture hall on Friday, however, I didn't see any students prompting ChatGPT.
In many ways, the class resembled a typical early morning university lecture (for undergrads, 10 a.m. is basically the crack of dawn). Sweatshirted students arrived late and filtered in the upper rows, while the overachievers sat in the front and asked questions.
Many bent their heads over large iPads and took furious notes while Yi filled up blackboard after blackboard with formulas and practice problems. Some had no note-taking materials to speak of. A couple closed their eyes for extended periods.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The class is a "core requirement" in Caltech's curriculum, meaning everyone at the school has to take it. Students I spoke to afterward gave a variety of majors, but none said they were comfortable speaking on the record.
So later on I spoke with Sathvik Redrouthu, a sophomore who'd taken the class last year. Redrouthu, a math major , said he didn't use AI because he wanted to understand the concepts.
"I was interested in the class," he said, adding that mainlining the homework with AI is like "shooting yourself in the foot" for when an in-person exam comes around.
"I personally think that if you leave AI out, then it pushes the average student to learn properly," he said.
If you're not interested in math, though, Redrouthu said you'd probably turn to AI — and you'd get away with it, until the exam at least.
Ni told me that, as a professor, he can't tell whether a problem set he assigns is completed using AI. It's unlike AI-generated writing, which is usually a pretty obvious amalgamation of short sentences, em dashes, and hypophora.
But math is all numbers: the specialty of AI programs .
Caltech has no unified guidance for how math professors should plan around AI now. Redrouthu said that this year, some of his classes come with an auspicious caveat: "AI allowed."
"Syllabuses are changing," he said.

articles.title_orig: Russia says its air defenses intercept over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in massive aerial attack
articles.title_zh: Russia says its air defenses intercept over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in massive aerial attack
articles.content_orig:
The Kerch bridge was built in 2018 and is one of President Putin's signature infrastructure projects (file photo)
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.
The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia's mainland with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.
The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate  has responded to a BBC request for comment.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.
Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and measures to ensure Kyiv's neutrality.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.
The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.
EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

articles.title_orig: Americans are ditching a longtime weekly tradition as restaurant dining hits record low
articles.title_zh: Americans are ditching a longtime weekly tradition as restaurant dining hits record low
articles.content_orig:
​Teneshia Murray Butler, owner of T's Brunch Bar in Atlanta, discusses declining restaurant traffic, changing customer habits and how economic uncertainty is affecting her business.
For many Americans, eating out at a restaurant is becoming more of an occasional treat than a weekly routine, according to a new poll.
The share of U.S. adults who say they eat at a restaurant at least once a week fell to 39% in 2026, according to a new Gallup poll , marking a record low in the organization's tracking.
That's down from 47% in 2022 and 53% in 2019, before the pandemic, according to the survey, which was conducted in early July.
MORE AMERICANS ARE DINING ALONE AS SOLO RESTAURANT RESERVATIONS SOAR, DATA SHOWS
People aren't abandoning dining out altogether, but the share who eat out only a few times a year has doubled from 10% to 20% since 2019. Only 4% of respondents said they never eat at restaurants . Online grocery ordering, meanwhile, is up 15% while weekly in-person grocery shopping has fallen to a record low of 74%.
Americans are dining out less often, with 39% saying they eat at a restaurant at least once a week, a new Gallup poll found.
Takeout orders aren't filling the gap either, the poll found. Weekly takeout ordering, which peaked at 39% in 2021, has returned to 31%, the same as it was in 2018.
Atlanta restaurateur Teneshia Murray Butler, owner of T’s Brunch Bar, has noticed business slow at her locations over the past four or five months. Dine-in and takeout traffic have both softened, she said, with weekdays especially slow.
THE 24-HOUR AMERICAN DINER IS VANISHING — HERE'S WHAT'S DRIVING THE DECLINE
"It’s just [fewer] people coming in," Murray Butler told Fox News Digital.
While she finds that customers are still ordering popular dishes and spending about the same per plate, she has noticed fewer families with children dining out.
The share of Americans who dine out weekly has fallen from 53% in 2019 to 39% in 2026, according to Gallup. (iStock)
She said going out to eat once a week was common when she was growing up, but she now sees fewer families with children and more couples or double dates.
Brandy Rand, vice president of hospitality at Forge, which produces the Bar & Restaurant Expo in Las Vegas, said value and the occasion both shape customers' decisions.
ALL-YOU-CAN-EAT DINING MAKES A COMEBACK AS AMERICANS LOOK FOR MORE BANG FOR THEIR BUCK
In a recent consumer habits survey by Forge, 42% of respondents said promotions or deals matter to them. The top reason people gave for dining out was treating themselves — cited by 53%.
"I don't think people are giving up on restaurants — they’re being selective about when and where they go," Rand said. She said takeout can't fully recreate the restaurant experience, including the drinks and social time that often come with a meal out.
Dine-in and takeout traffic at T's Brunch Bar have slowed in recent months, but specials have helped draw diners in. (T's Brunch Bar)
Murray Butler said she offers specials to draw customers in on slow days, including $5 drinks and $10 meals , along with other deals. "I have lamb chops for $5 for one. … They might order four lamb chops and a side order, and it's cheaper than ordering the whole meal."
Gallup found the latest decline was concentrated among middle- and upper-income adults. Weekly dining fell to 38% among middle-income adults and 48% among upper-income adults. Among lower-income adults, it held at 32%, the lowest of the three groups.
RESTAURANTS BRING BACK OLD-SCHOOL HOSPITALITY AS NOSTALGIA TAKES HOLD ACROSS AMERICA
Murray Butler noted costs have risen, too, including for beef, frying batter and takeout supplies.
Rising food and supply costs are adding to the challenges restaurant owners face as some customers cut back on dining out. (iStock)
Higher prices may be one factor, Gallup said, but may not explain everything. The poll was conducted during a major cyclospora outbreak linked to produce served at some restaurants, and Gallup noted that food-safety concerns could have influenced responses.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Customers were worried about contaminated lettuce, and so was Murray Butler.
"I didn't even want to serve it on a cheeseburger. ... I was so scared because it was on the news and everywhere," she added, explaining that she had to check labels on incoming lettuce and ask her vendor to ensure it had been properly inspected.
"You [have to] make people remember your restaurant."
Americans' confidence in food safety has hit a new low, a separate Gallup survey from September found, with 73% of people saying they have avoided certain foods in the past year because of a recall or advisory.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
For restaurants, the challenge may be persuading customers that a visit is worth the expense, experts say. Rand said deals, special menus and reliable service all help give diners a reason to return.
Restaurant operators are offering specials and promotions to give customers more reasons to dine out, hospitality experts say. (iStock)
"I think you're [going to have] to tell people why they should come to my restaurant," Murray Butler agreed. "'I have this happy hour special. I have this item. I have new menu items.'"
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
She advertises T's Brunch Bar on billboards throughout Atlanta and said she is pursuing additional placements at the airport to keep the restaurant top of mind when people decide where to eat.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"You just got to market in people's face everywhere," she said. "You [have to] make people remember your restaurant."
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
articles.title_zh: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
articles.content_orig:
It's on us. Share your news here.
Posted on November 16, 2026
India’s push to expand domestic shipbuilding and lessen its dependence on China has found an eager partner in Korea, whose shipbuilders are looking for new production bases abroad.
Those complementary needs are driving a burgeoning partnership centered on Thoothukudi, a port city near India’s southern tip, where HD Hyundai plans to build a $4 billion shipyard with Indian state partners. On India’s west coast, Samsung Heavy Industries is backing an Indian yard competing for the country’s first oil tanker orders in decades.
The stakes reach beyond the two countries. China, Korea and Japan accounted for about 93 percent of global shipbuilding in 2024, according to Clarksons Research, and India is spending public money to become the fourth name on that list, with Korean partners instead of Chinese ones.
When India’s shipping minister visited Korea last month, he toured Korean shipyards and explored business opportunities with all three of Korea’s major shipbuilders, underscoring New Delhi’s push to expand its shipbuilding industry.
India’s Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal met HD Hyundai Chairman Chung Ki-sun, Samsung Heavy Industries CEO Choi Sung-an and Hanwha Ocean Executive Vice President Kim Chang-yong to ask for investment and technology transfer during a four-day trip that ended Oct. 28.
The tour was the latest in a series of attempts by New Delhi to import an industry it has not managed to build on its own. India ranks 12th in global shipbuilding and wants to be in the top five by 2047.
For Korean yards that are full at home and losing orders to China, it is a subsidized way to add capacity. The outcome will show whether a shipbuilding industry can be assembled outside East Asia from state funding and borrowed know-how.
About 95 percent of India’s trade by volume moves by sea, the country spends close to $75 billion a year hiring foreign ships, and its own yards held 0.5 percent of the global order book as of Sept. 1, according to the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO).
Indian cabinet earmarked 697.3 billion rupees ($7.4 billion) in September 2025 to lift annual capacity to 4.5 million gross tons by 2047. State-run buyers plan to order 437 vessels worth about 2.2 trillion rupees.
Demand is not the constraint but the ability to build is. Indian yards delivered about 65,000 deadweight tons of ships in the fiscal year through March 2025, roughly a fifth of a single supertanker. Cheap labor does not close the gap. An Indian yard needs 150 to 180 man-hours for work that takes 10 to 15 in Korea, Han Seung-han, an analyst at SK Securities, wrote in a September report.
“A policy of adding capacity does not by itself raise the ability to build ships,” Han wrote. “The capability to run a yard has to come in whole.”
Korean yards face the reverse problem. The industry is in a supercycle, and “domestic production capacity is almost full, with work backed up three to five years,” said Lee Kyu-seok, a senior research fellow at the Export-Import Bank of Korea’s Overseas Economic Research Institute. India, he added, appears to offer “a structure where it is easier to match production costs.”
Nor would Indian yards serve only India. “Shipbuilding is already globalized,” Lee said.
Among the partners India could have chosen, China, the largest builder, seems ruled out. “Because of the border dispute, India does not cooperate with China in strategic industries,” said Kim Kyung-hoon, head of the India and South Asia team at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.
New Delhi has thawed ties with Beijing, hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit in September, but relations remain far from the level needed for industrial cooperation, he said. “Handing shipbuilding subsidies to China is unimaginable.”
Japan’s yards have moved on to specialized vessels, while India wants to start with container ships and large oil tankers, which Korean yards still build, Kim said. “Korea is almost the only partner.”
A similar rivalry looks to be pushing Korea toward India. Chinese yards won 63 percent of global new orders last year and Korean yards 21 percent, according to Clarksons Research. Korean builders now see Southeast Asia and India as partners that can help offset China, an industry representative familiar with the matter said.
“After Southeast Asia, India is the market drawing attention,” the representative said, adding that India is courting Korea’s three major shipbuilders to grow its own industry.
HD Hyundai is leading Korean shipbuilders’ foray into India. When Sonowal met Chung on Oct. 28, the two sides agreed to finish a detailed project report (DPR) on the yard’s cost, size and schedule within six months. The local port authority ordered a feasibility study in September, and site inspections are now underway.
HD Hyundai is to run the yard through a joint venture as its largest shareholder. Until it opens, India plans to place its first orders with HD Hyundai’s yards in Korea and send workers there for training. The partnership began with a Tamil Nadu state agreement in December 2025.
“The specific shareholding structure and investment size of the joint venture are under discussion with the relevant agencies and partners,” HD Hyundai said in a written response to the Korea JoongAng Daily. “However, under the [memorandum of understanding] signed among equity investors on the occasion of the Korea-India summit in April, our baseline is to secure at least 60 percent of the joint venture.”
What HD Hyundai gains is scale it cannot add at home. The yard is planned to turn out about 2.5 million gross tons a year, more than half of the capacity India wants nationwide by 2047. It would be the group’s third overseas base after Vietnam and the Philippines, and subsidies would carry much of the cost: Han estimates that central and state support will cover 45 to 47 percent of the $4 billion bill, leaving HD Hyundai to fund about $2.2 billion.
“We are looking to build a stable production system by securing both Indian domestic orders and global orders,” the company said. “Over the long term, we expect it to diversify our global production system by drawing on India’s abundant work force and growth potential, and to complement the production capacity of our domestic yards.”
Han expects the next round of global orders to center on tankers and bulk carriers, where competing with China comes down to cost. Nearly half of India’s 1,592 ships are more than 20 years old, and most are tankers or bulk carriers, he noted. “It cannot be solved with domestic yards,” Han wrote. “The answer is India, following Vietnam and the Philippines.”
Samsung Heavy Industries has taken a lighter route, lending know-how to an existing Indian yard instead of building one. It signed a cooperation deal in September 2025 with Swan Defence and Heavy Industries. Last month, Swan submitted the lowest bid for up to four product tankers for a venture led by the state-run Shipping Corporation of India, undercutting a Cochin Shipyard bid backed by HD Hyundai. The contract has not been finalized. Hanwha Ocean has so far held talks with state-run Hindustan Shipyard on ship design.
The agreements remain nonbinding, and investment terms and construction dates are still open.
The larger risk lies in India’s follow-through. The yard would take four to five years to build, Kim said, and until then New Delhi and Tamil Nadu have to keep paying subsidies, acquiring land and ordering ships through state firms. “Whether it keeps ordering ships as planned is the question mark,” Kim said. “How binding that cooperation becomes is the biggest question.”
The subsidies also have an end date. India’s shipbuilding aid is scheduled to run until March 2036, so a yard finished around 2031 would have about five years of assured support. “The 20 to 30 percent subsidies offset the cost gap,” Han wrote. “They do not resolve it structurally.”

articles.title_orig: The Investors Set to Win Big in Anthropic’s IPO
articles.title_zh: The Investors Set to Win Big in Anthropic’s IPO
articles.content_orig:
Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.
Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.
With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.
Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.
"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."
Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.
By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.
The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Google didn't provide a comment.
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

articles.title_orig: China says Xi, Trump, Putin to discuss 'world peace'
articles.title_zh: China says Xi, Trump, Putin to discuss 'world peace'
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures slide as Nvidia leads AI stocks lower: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures slide as Nvidia leads AI stocks lower: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures fell on Monday, dragged down by key technology stocks, as traders awaited a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut of Anthropic this week.
Nasdaq-100 futures declined 1.5%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.7%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures shed 55 points, or 0.1%.
Shares in Nvidia were down about 4% in premarket trading as the embattled chipmaker prepares to report its third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the company to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
Over the weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a " dramatic shakeup " at Nvidia, urging its board to look outside the company for its next CEO.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter."
Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade were under pressure along with Nvidia. Fellow chipmakers Micron Technology , Intel and Advanced Micro Devices each lost more than 5%. Additionally, shares of computer maker Dell Technologies also declined more than 5%, while software stock Oracle moved down nearly 4%.
Another key test for the trade this week is Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week despite Nvidia's tumble. The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly gains since August, rising more than 2% each.
In Asia, markets closed mostly lower Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 dropping 2.42% after third-quarter GDP unexpectedly shrank. South Korea's Kospi slumped 3.59%, leading losses in the region. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.41%. Mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.91% after downbeat key economic data, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index gained 0.49%.
In Europe, the pan-European Stoxx 600 was up 0.12%. The U.K. FTSE 100 rose 0.28%, while France's CAC 40 advanced 0.30%. Germany's DAX was just above the flatline.
UniCredit 's takeover of Commerzbank has been given the go-ahead by European competition regulators.
The European Commission on Monday gave antitrust approval to the Italian lender's bid to take control of its German peer, following similar consent from the European Central Bank last month.
That now clears the path for the takeover, with UniCredit's integration plan expected to begin early next year.
"Our approval of UniCredit's acquisition of Commerzbank shows that it is possible to support a stronger European banking sector while safeguarding competition and choice," said Teresa Ribera, the Commission's first executive vice-president for a clean, just and competitive transition.
Shares in Milan-listed UniCredit were 0.62% lower in morning trade. Commerzbank was down 1% in Frankfurt.
Nvidia 's stock fell 1.72% in premarket trading, continuing its slide after losing hundreds of billions in market cap last week amid the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as CEO.
Nvidia announced Huang was stepping down as CEO on Thursday, amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a spy for China. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday.
Oil prices moved higher on Monday, with Brent crude — the global price benchmark — rising 0.30% to $96.13 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures added 0.49% to $89.03.
The rise comes after two oil tankers reportedly struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters, which cited Iran's Revolutionary Guard. It followed similar reported incidents on Sunday and Monday.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was almost 0.1% higher in early dealmaking, as most continental sectors made gains and major bourses were mixed shortly after 8:10 a.m. in London (3:10 a.m. E.T.).
Healthcare stocks advanced 0.79%, followed by telecommunications, which were up 0.67%, as household goods gained 0.63%. Basic resources shed 1.67%
Among regional bourses, the French CAC 40 led early gains, rising 0.30%, while the U.K. FTSE 100 added 0.22%. Germany's DAX fell 0.10%, and the Italian FTSE MIB was 0.39% down.
European stock markets are expected to start the new trading week in mostly negative territory.
Stoxx 50 futures seen opening almost 0.1% lower, with all of the continent's major bourses in the red.
The French CAC 40 was almost 0.2% down ahead of Monday's session, while the Italian FTSE MIB was about 0.1% lower.
Futures tied to the U.K. FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX were seen opening around the flatline.
Asian tech heavyweights slid on Monday as investors continued to grapple with the fallout from developments at chip giant Nvidia, with former CEO Jensen Huang reportedly mulling a dramatic comeback.
Key Nvidia suppliers Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company all plunged, with SK Hynix down over 5.6%. Samsung and TSMC lost about 3% each.
AI-related stocks in Japan saw larger losses, with Advantest plunging almost 10% and Tokyo Electron falling 5.2%. Softbank Group Corp , a major AI investor, declined 4.2%.
China's economic slowdown worsened in October with retail sales, investment and industrial output all missing economists' estimates, as analysts warn the growing reliance on external drivers is deepening structural imbalances.
Monday's data showed the investment slump deepened and retail sales again lagged industrial output, as consumer spending languished with the property market downturn eroding household wealth for a fifth year.
The economic malaise also weighed on the labor market. Unemployment inched lower to 5.1% in October, while the jobless rate for those aged between 16 and 24, excluding students, hovered near the highest level in a year, standing at 18% in September.
Japan's economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, shrinking at an annualized 0.1% compared to the previous quarter, as elevated energy prices impacted consumption and net exports.
A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3% in the three months to September, while GDP had expanded at 1.4% in the previous quarter.
While Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, net exports weighed on the economy due to higher costs of energy imports, cutting 0.6 percentage point from the country's growth.
Markets in Asia opened lower Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 leading losses among the major indexes after its third-quarter GDP unexpectedly contracted.
Nikkei fell 0.63%, while the broad-based Topix dropped 0.24%.
South Korea Kospi fell 0.1%, while the small-cap Kosdaq was 0.56% lower. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.12% as well.
Nikkei 225 and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index were set to open higher Monday, with focus on key economic data out of Japan and mainland China.
China is expected to release data for retail sales, industrial output and urban unemployment for October later in the day, while Japan will release economic growth data.
Japan is expected to see GDP growth slow sharply to an annualized 0.3% for the third quarter, compared to 1.4% in the quarter before, according to Reuters estimates.

articles.title_orig: Trump heads to Asia for 2nd high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi amid Nvidia CEO scandal - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to Asia for 2nd high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi amid Nvidia CEO scandal - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Questions remain about the Nvidia CEO's relationship with alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.
This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions.
The tariffs have been ensnared in legal challenges in count -- and Democrats, who will take the majority in January, have vowed to counter them and reassert congressional authority over trade. They don’t have a veto-proof majority, however, and Trump has vowed to use his veto pen to kill bills he doesn't like.
And the president does not appear to feel pressure to reign in his sweeping tariffs. On Nov. 12,

articles.title_orig: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
articles.title_zh: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
articles.content_orig:
This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you.
That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year.
Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information.
Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out.
If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January.
Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC.
Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email , text message or phone call claiming to be from HMRC is genuine.
"Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer.
New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October.
There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information.
To avoid being caught out, HMRC says:
In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered.
Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy.
"When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check.
"No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy."

articles.title_orig: Mexican president arrives in China for APEC summit, set to meet Xi
articles.title_zh: Mexican president arrives in China for APEC summit, set to meet Xi
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: The Lost Roman Legion That Vanished into Ancient China
articles.title_zh: The Lost Roman Legion That Vanished into Ancient China
articles.content_orig:
It is rumored that in 53 BC, thousands of Roman soldiers vanished after the Battle of Carrhae, and that the survivors settled in Han Dynasty China.
Published: Nov 16, 2026 written by Robert De Graaff , MA History
Published: Nov 16, 2026 written by Robert De Graaff , MA History
In 53 BC, ten thousand Roman legionaries vanished into the eastern deserts following the catastrophic Battle of Carrhae. Decades later, Chinese chroniclers recorded a mysterious foreign force fighting in a tight fish-scale formation thousands of miles away on the Silk Road. Did survivors of Rome’s worst defeat march across Asia to found a remote village in Han Dynasty China? What is the evidence to support this popular but unproven theory?
In 1957, American academic Homer Dubs published a paper theorizing the presence of a Roman legion in ancient China. The story begins in 53 BC when Marcus Licinius Crassus launched an invasion of Parthia to enhance his military reputation. He was killed, and his army was smashed at the Battle of Carrhae , where thousands were killed, and thousands more were taken prisoner.
The Parthians , not wanting to waste the manpower, found a use for the prisoners. The captured Romans were given back their weapons and equipment and pressed into service. It may seem strange to rely on an enemy for national security, but this practice was very common throughout history, especially in the ancient world. It is something the Parthians were known for.
Obviously, stationing these troops on the western border with Roman territory was out of the question. The legionaries were shipped off to the east to the far-flung reaches of the Parthian empire. They would end up in Central Asia, guarding against bandits and other threats in what is now Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Any direct mention of these soldiers ends there, but this is only the first part of the story.
Seventeen years later, the Romans may reappear in the historical record. Far to the east, Han China was expanding, spreading further and further west, setting up the Western Protectorate, areas under Chinese influence if not outright control. The Chinese clashed with Parthia at Zhizhi, modern-day Kazakhstan, and won a decisive victory. This secured Han China’s western flank, establishing Chinese presence in the region.
Chinese records of the battle mention something interesting. Some of the soldiers they fought against used what was described as a fish-scale pattern formation. Some scholars believe this is the famous Roman testudo formation, in which legionaries interlock their shields to protect against missile attacks, resembling the overlapping scales of a fish.
The Chinese were impressed by these soldiers, and once again, the Romans were employed by their captors. They were moved even further east, along the Chinese- Tibetan border, to guard against raids. Specifically, they were moved to a place called Liqian, which shares the name the Chinese gave Rome, roughly translated as “people of the West.”
Many inhabitants of Liqian today have Caucasian DNA and traditionally European features, such as lighter skin, lighter-colored eyes, and prominent noses. They are also generally much taller than their ethnic Chinese countrymen. So, is this proof that the Romans reached China and fought for the Han Dynasty?
While all of this evidence may seem compelling, the theory falls apart under closer scrutiny. The name Liqian was the Han Chinese name for Rome, but the same name was used for the Greek kingdoms in Central Asia founded by Alexander the Great and his successors . More than likely, with such limited contact between them, the name was more of a generic term for those of European descent, without any consideration for ethnic subdivisions. The fish scale formation does sound a lot like the testudo , but this is circumstantial. While it may be Romans whom the Chinese fought at Zhizhi, it may have been soldiers who copied Roman ways, or it may be something else altogether. A simple phrase is hardly conclusive evidence.
A significant portion of the Liqian locals indeed have Caucasian genes, but did it come from Romans, or the Greek kingdoms in Central Asia, whose people could have migrated along the well-established trade routes to Liqian? The nomadic peoples of the Eurasian Steppe, which runs from Hungary to Korea, are also a hodgepodge of ethnic groups, so having Caucasian genes from this source is not out of the question.
In truth, the absence of evidence is evidence of absence. To date, there have been no archaeological finds that support the idea of a Roman legion in central China along the Tibetan border. There have been no finds of Roman weapons, armor, or other military equipment , no coins, no religious votive offerings, or anything else associated with a significant Roman population.
Over the past few decades, Homer Dub’s theory linking the various pieces of evidence has generated much debate among scholars and history enthusiasts, but for now, the evidence is circumstantial. The idea of the presence of Romans in China belongs more to the realm of fiction than fact.
Robert is a history enthusiast who specializes in military history and dabbles in many other topics of the past. He is also a script writer for a popular history-focused YouTube channel.

articles.title_orig: Carney heads to China to meet with President Xi, leaders from across Pacific Rim
articles.title_zh: Carney heads to China to meet with President Xi, leaders from across Pacific Rim
articles.content_orig:
PHNOM PENH — Prime Minister Mark Carney is travelling to China today, where he is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and leaders from across the Pacific Rim.
Carney is leaving the Francophonie summit in Cambodia and travelling to Shenzhen, China's tech hub, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit.
He is scheduled to meet with Xi at a time that will be Tuesday morning in China but late Monday evening in Ottawa. Carney said Canada could do more with China in terms of agriculture, clean and conventional energy, and financial services.
"We've established pretty clear guardrails on the areas that we're going to focus on … I'm using our words, not theirs," he told reporters in Phnom Penh.
Carney also expects to speak with Xi about "the evolution of the international system, China's role in that and Canadian priorities."
An overarching topic will be Chinese investments into Canada's auto sector. Both countries agreed earlier this year to allow a limited amount of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada.
Carney has said he wants Chinese carmakers to set up shop, but only if they provide decent jobs, saying he is wary of plants where workers assemble cars using components mostly made in China.
He said trade talks with Washington will shape how Canada approaches Chinese investment.
"It's part of the trade negotiations," he said. "Depending (on) where that settles, there'll be other options — European options, Asian options."
"This is not leverage, but you know, action-reaction. It depends."
Carney will also meet with various leaders from the APEC forum, a group of 21 economies on both sides of the Pacific that work together to break down trade barriers. The grouping includes members as varied as Taiwan, Australia and Peru.
Carney's office says he will stick with his focus of drumming up more investment and diversifying Canadian trade.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said she'll be watching to see whether Carney allows more Chinese investments into Canada "in critical sectors, in energy and technology, particularly related to renewables and batteries" in addition to auto manufacturing.
"We have to constantly triangulate our relationship with China with our discussions with the U.S. — and also watch then what happens between the U.S. and China bilaterally," she said.
Nadjibulla also said the summit should help craft the foreign policy review that Carney aims to table in the House of Commons in the coming weeks, as well as next year's planned renewal of the 2022 Indo-Pacific strategy launched by his predecessor Justin Trudeau.
"We now have a really solid foundation," Nadjibulla said, noting that leaders from Asia have visited Canada or are planning to, notably Vietnam and India.
"Canada is finally on their radar and has relevance to their own diversification agendas and their own economic security and resilience agendas."
She said any update to Ottawa's regional strategy must include a look at relations with Taiwan, a self-governing island which China claims. The federal cabinet has left a trade arrangement sitting unsigned for more than a year, despite the House foreign-affairs committee urging that government proceed with more economic relations.
During the APEC summit, U.S. President Donald Trump is set to meet President Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
That has raised alarm among European officials, as some suggest U.S.-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine have included proposals they say would leave both Ukraine and Europe vulnerable.
Carney said Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva recently told him that he encouraged the talks in order to end the war. Carney said Canada wants a just peace for Ukraine and a ceasefire is needed.
Nadjibulla said it's incredible the trilateral meeting might happen, adding that it reinforces Carney's warnings about "unconstrained great-power politics" in his January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos.
"It's a reminder that other countries need to double down on their efforts to build resilience and agency, so that they don't become collateral — so they don't end up on the menu of great-power competition, but rather have a seat at the table," she said.
China has indicated great enthusiasm for Carney's visit. The state-controlled English-language newspaper Global Times has framed it as a mutually beneficial partnership in a turbulent world.
"The ability of China and Canada to address previous trade frictions through calm and equal-footed dialogue not only helps strengthen bilateral strategic mutual trust, but also injects confidence into global economic and trade co-operation," said Zhao Xingshu of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, according to the newspaper.
"Nearly eight years of limited high-level exchanges mean rebuilding mutual understanding between officials and institutions will require time. At this stage, maintaining the momentum of stabilization in bilateral relations is itself an important and realistic objective."
The APEC summit takes place in Shenzhen, which borders Hong Kong, where Canada has repeatedly expressed concern about growing repression as the territory transitions from semi-autonomy to full Chinese rule.
Earlier this month, Canada joined western peers in condemning 10-year sentences for politicians and democracy activists under national-security laws, particularly Joshua Wong.
"We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the (national security law)," the joint statement says.
It urges Chinese leaders to "uphold their international commitments and honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong" when the British government ceded sovereignty.
Carney has said he raises human rights issues privately with China but avoids public criticism.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.
Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

articles.title_orig: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back from Bab el-Mandeb Strait as rebels advance towards Aden
articles.title_zh: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back from Bab el-Mandeb Strait as rebels advance towards Aden
articles.content_orig:
The Southern Armed Forces group allied with Yemen's UN-recognized government and backed by Saudi Arabia said Sunday they had repositioned themselves away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Southern Armed Forces said the repositioning is intended to secure the southern city of Aden, "and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the frontlines and addressing existing threats."
Aden, which has a population of over a million people, is the interim seat of the Yemeni government, formally known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC).
The Southern Armed Forces also intend to end the Houthi siege over the strategic southwestern city of Taiz.
Nearly two million people live in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
The siege is raising fears of famine for residents, as well as a possible medical crisis as hospitals face restricted supplies.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The Houthis control much of northwest Yemen , including the capital Sanaa.
The rebels are a Shiite militant group backed by Iran. The US, Canada and several other countries regard them as a terror organization.
The Houthis in September launched a rapid offensive against the PLC, seizing much of the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
It is also a key corridor for maritime trade and energy shipments.
The Houthis have taken control of the major port town of Mocha in September, firming their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The latest redeployment of the Southern Armed Forces is likely to give the rebels even more control over the strategic area.
Sources told AFP news agency that Houthi forces are now just 60 kilometers (less than 40 miles) from Aden.
The conflict between the Yemeni government and the Houthis has lasted for over 10 years.
The fighting in Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, has been fueled by the wider rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In recent weeks, the Houthis have been launching frequent attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, the rebels claimed that they targeted the King Khalid International Airport and financial district of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the alleged Houthi attack.
